blocks.text: Ephesians 2 presents a narrative of transformation: from spiritual death to life in Christ, from alienation to reconciliation, from division to unity. Written to Gentile believers, the chapter emphasizes how divine grace and Christ's reconciling peace create one new humanity from Jews and Gentiles. This movement from death to life, from separation to belonging, illustrates the redemptive shape of God's plan and invites believers to understand their place within God's unified people.

The opening verses describe the spiritual condition of believers before Christ: dead through trespasses and sins. Sin here—in Hebrew and Greek usage rendered as hamartia—carries varied meaning depending on context. In this passage it represents both the state of disobedience and active rebellion. Believers once walked according to the course of this world and the desires of the flesh, living under the influence of spiritual powers opposed to God, and were by nature children of wrath—a condition shared by all humanity.

The passage pivots sharply with 'But God.' God, rich in mercy and acting out of great love, reverses the condition of death. The language here draws on a deep biblical tradition of divine mercy—hesed and eleos in Hebrew and Greek—concepts that Scripture develops from Israel's story into the New Testament witness. God makes believers alive together with Christ, raises them up, and seats them in the heavenly places. This union with Christ establishes a new status in the present while pointing toward the full revelation of God's grace in the ages to come.

Verses 8-10 explicitly ground salvation in grace received through faith, stating it is not 'of yourselves' but 'the gift of God,' and not earned by works. The passage joins this salvation by grace with the claim that believers are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works that God has prepared beforehand. The grammar does not definitively establish whether faith itself is identified as the gift, but the central assertion is clear: salvation comes from God as grace, apprehended through faith, not from human achievement.

The passage now addresses the Gentile audience directly, recalling their former status: separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants of promise, without hope and without God in the world. This historical reminder—stark in its portrayal of complete spiritual exclusion—grounds the magnitude of the reconciliation that follows. The passage develops the theme of the people of God across Scripture, highlighting the significance of the transformation that Christ has wrought.
